title: Data & Compute
oneLineScope: The corpora behind the first large language models — BooksCorpus, Wikipedia, WebText, C4 — and the compute story that connects them to scaling laws.
prose:
The transformer architecture, the pretraining objectives, and the optimization recipes described in the preceding nodes are machinery. What drives that machinery is unlabeled text in industrial quantities and the compute to process it. This node catalogs what was actually used — which corpora, which approximate scales, who scraped or filtered them — and frames the compute story that node 18 (scaling laws) will quantify. The figures here are worth understanding not as magic numbers but as a record of how the field's ambitions grew when it discovered that more data and more compute reliably improved loss.

The corpora

BooksCorpus (Zhu et al., 2015) was assembled to study cross-modal alignment — aligning books with their film adaptations — but it became foundational to language model pretraining almost incidentally. The corpus consists of over 7,000 unpublished novels scraped from a self-publishing platform. Zhu et al. report approximately 800 million words. Two properties made it attractive for pretraining beyond its size: the texts are long-form, with coherent narrative structure across thousands of tokens, providing exactly the kind of long-range dependency training data that short web snippets cannot; and the distribution of topics and register is relatively clean, since books that reach publication (even self-publication) tend toward grammatical prose. GPT-1 (Radford et al., 2018) was pretrained on BooksCorpus alone; BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) trained on BooksCorpus combined with English Wikipedia.

English Wikipedia (as used in BERT) contributed roughly 2.5 billion words at the time of BERT's training, per Devlin et al.'s description. Wikipedia text is clean, factual, encyclopedic in register, and densely cross-referenced — a different distributional profile from novels. Combining it with BooksCorpus gave BERT both long-form narrative and structured factual text, which plausibly accounts for some of the breadth of what BERT's representations encode. The combined corpus is modest by later standards — on the order of 3 billion words total — but it was sufficient to demonstrate that large-scale bidirectional pretraining produced representations competitive with or superior to task-specific architectures across many NLP benchmarks.

WebText was assembled for GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019). Rather than crawling the web indiscriminately, the authors used a quality heuristic: they scraped all outbound links from Reddit posts that had received at least 3 upvotes (karma). The intuition is that human curation — even the low bar of three Reddit upvotes — filters toward text someone found interesting or informative enough to share. The resulting corpus is approximately 40 GB of text (about 8 million documents), and Radford et al. describe it as WebText. This is considerably larger than BooksCorpus plus Wikipedia, and its web-native distribution — news, blogs, technical writing, fiction, forum posts — is closer to the range of text a general-purpose language model will encounter at inference. WebText is not publicly released; an approximate open recreation is called OpenWebText.

C4 — the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus — was constructed by Raffel et al. (2020) for T5. The starting point is Common Crawl, a publicly available, continuously updated crawl of the web that runs to petabytes of raw HTML. Common Crawl is enormous but extremely noisy: it contains deduplication artifacts, boilerplate, non-English text, and outright garbage. Raffel et al. applied a sequence of filters — removing pages without sentence-ending punctuation, deduplicating at the three-sentence-span level, discarding pages containing offensive language from a blocklist, keeping only English pages — to produce C4. After filtering, C4 is hundreds of gigabytes of text (Raffel et al. describe the English C4 as approximately 750 GB). The published paper's §2 describes the filtering pipeline in careful detail; that section is worth reading because it makes concrete just how much of the raw web is discarded and how sensitive the resulting corpus quality is to filtering decisions.

The throughline across these four corpora is one of scale, diversity, and quality filtering. BooksCorpus: small, clean, long-form. Wikipedia: small, clean, factual. WebText: medium, quality-heuristic-filtered web. C4: large, aggressively filtered web. Each step outward on the scale axis required new cleaning infrastructure, and the community's experience with C4 made clear that indiscriminate scaling — taking Common Crawl at face value — does not work. Deduplication and quality filtering are not preprocessing details; they materially affect the model's downstream behavior. A model trained on deduplicated data memorizes the training set less and generalizes better, a point that subsequent work (Hernandez et al., Lee et al., and others) would examine more carefully.

The compute story

Training these models moved from single-machine GPU runs to large multi-accelerator jobs during the GPT-1 to BERT to GPT-2 period. GPT-1 was trained on 8 GPUs; BERT was trained on 64 TPU v2 chips (Devlin et al., §3.1 describes this explicitly); GPT-2 required a compute cluster whose full specification Radford et al. do not publish in detail. The qualitative shift — from hardware a single researcher could plausibly rent to hardware requiring dedicated infrastructure — happened over roughly two years, 2018–2019.

A useful approximate relationship, introduced in the scaling-laws literature, connects compute \(C\) (in floating-point operations), parameter count \(N\), and training token count \(D\):

\[ C \approx 6 N D \]

Here \(C\) is total training FLOPs, \(N\) is the number of model parameters, and \(D\) is the number of tokens processed during training. The factor of 6 accounts for the forward pass, the backward pass (which is approximately twice the cost of the forward), and the parameter-update step; the derivation and the conditions under which this approximation holds are in Kaplan et al. (2020), §2.1. It is an approximation, not an identity: it ignores embedding layers and attention's \(n^2\) term, which are sub-dominant for moderate sequence lengths. But it is accurate to within a small constant for the dense transformer architectures in this era, and it is the right handle to reach for when you want to reason about the order of magnitude of a training run from a paper's reported parameter count and token count.

To put rough numbers to it (with the caveat that exact GPU-hours from these papers are not always published and the following are order-of-magnitude estimates): a BERT-base model (\(N \approx 110\)M parameters) trained on roughly 1 billion tokens implies \(C \approx 6 \times 1.1 \times 10^8 \times 10^9 \approx 6.6 \times 10^{17}\) FLOPs. GPT-2 (\(N \approx 1.5\)B) on WebText's roughly 10 billion tokens gives \(C \approx 9 \times 10^{19}\) FLOPs. These numbers are large but tractable on the hardware of the era; they became less tractable as GPT-3 (175B parameters, 300B tokens) pushed into the \(3 \times 10^{23}\) FLOP range. At that scale, compute cost, not algorithm design, became the binding constraint on experimentation.

The appetite of these models for unlabeled text and compute is precisely what node 18 (scaling laws) quantifies as a power law. The empirical observation that loss decreases predictably as \(N\), \(D\), and \(C\) grow — over many orders of magnitude — gave the field a framework for planning training runs: given a compute budget, how should it be split between a larger model and more data? The \(C \approx 6ND\) relationship is the bridge between that question and the practical choices made in dataset construction and hardware allocation. Understanding the corpora and the compute story here is the prerequisite for reading Kaplan et al. with full appreciation of what they were measuring.

Four datasets are marked as points or segments: BooksCorpus (~800M words, used by GPT-1 and BERT), English Wikipedia (~2.5B words, used by BERT), WebText (~40GB / ~8B tokens, used by GPT-2), and C4 (~750GB after filtering, used by T5). Each dataset label includes its source attribution. An annotation notes that C4 started from Common Crawl (petabytes) but was filtered down to hundreds of GB.

diagrams.caption: The pretraining pipeline: raw text passes through cleaning and deduplication, becomes a tokenized corpus, and feeds pretraining under a compute budget governed approximately by C ≈ 6ND.
diagrams.altText: A left-to-right pipeline with four stages. Stage 1: raw web and book text (labeled 'raw text'). Stage 2: a cleaning and deduplication box, annotated with example steps (language filter, deduplicate, quality filter). Stage 3: a tokenized corpus box, labeled with vocabulary size V and token count D. Stage 4: a pretraining box consuming compute C, with the approximation C ≈ 6ND labeled inside or beside it, and N (parameters) feeding in from below. An arrow from stage 4 leads to a trained model on the right.

Stage 4: a box labeled 'pretraining' with the formula C ≈ 6ND written inside; an additional small box or arrow labeled 'model (N parameters)' feeds into this stage from below or the side. An arrow from stage 4 leads to a final box on the right labeled 'pretrained model'. Emphasize the cleaning step (stage 2) in red as the key quality gate; the tokenized corpus (stage 3) in blue as the thing under construction; the pretrained model output in green.

bibliography.citation: Zhu, Y., et al. (2015). "Aligning Books and Movies: Towards Story-Like Visual Explanations by Watching Movies and Reading Books." ICCV. arXiv:1506.06724.
bibliography.annotation: Source of BooksCorpus. §3.1 describes the corpus collection. The paper's primary goal is cross-modal alignment, not language modeling — the corpus became important incidentally. Cite for the ~800M-word figure and the long-form narrative property.

bibliography.citation: Radford, A., et al. (2019). "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners." OpenAI Blog (GPT-2 paper).
bibliography.annotation: Source of the WebText corpus description: §2.2 describes the Reddit-link scraping heuristic, the ≥3 karma filter, and the ~40GB size. GPT-2 architecture and byte-level BPE are also described here.

bibliography.citation: Raffel, C., et al. (2020). "Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer." JMLR 21(140). arXiv:1910.10683.
bibliography.annotation: Source of C4 and the T5 model. §2 describes the full Common Crawl filtering pipeline in careful detail — this is the authoritative reference for what cleaning steps were applied and why. The paper also provides a systematic study of pretraining objectives and dataset choices.

bibliography.citation: Kaplan, J., et al. (2020). "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models." arXiv:2001.08361.
bibliography.annotation: Source of the C ≈ 6ND approximation (§2.1). The paper derives the factor of 6 and discusses its domain of validity. This is also the primary source for node 18; reading §2 of Kaplan et al. alongside this node provides the bridge from corpus/compute facts to the power-law framework.
